newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open higher ahead of jobless data.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open higher ahead of jobless data.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices opened higher, in line with overseas trends, as the market waited for weekly data on U.S. jobless claims.
"The market got minor support in Europe," said David Sloan, senior domestic economist at I.D.E.A. "It's really waiting for the economic data today."

The government will report jobless claims data for the week ended January 11. Economists polled by Reuters forecast, on average, that new claims slipped to 355,000 in the latest week from 361,000 a week earlier.
Sloan said he expected a modest rise in claims, to 365,000 from 361,000 in the previous week.
"That would maintain the recent uptrend," he said. "At this time there are no obvious distortions in the data so this could be a more legitimate figure."
Economists said data for the weeks ended December 28 and Janaury 4 were harder to evaluate since each of those weeks was bisected by a holiday -- Christmas or New Year's Day.
U.S. jobless claims figures are due at 0830 EST/1330 GMT.
The only other economic data the market will examine this session is the January Philadelphia Federal Reserve survey.
Economists offered an average forecast of +4.8, versus December's reading of -2.2 for the Philadelphia report, which surveys business conditions in the Philadelphia region.

Traders said comments from Federal Reserve Governor Laurence Meyer in a "Nightly Business Report" broadcast on public television were market friendly. Meyer said he expected energy prices to moderate in the coming months.
Meyer will discuss the economic outlook and monetary policy at a luncheon sponsored by the Charlotte Economics Club in Charlotte, N.C. at 1230 EST/1730 GMT.
"Meyer doesn't seem to be one of the more hawkish members of the Fed," said Sloan. "His remarks are not likely to hurt the market."
Traders and analysts said the market's ability to advance even on friendly economic data on Thursday should be constrained by awareness that more influential events and economic data lie ahead.
"Industrial production (due Friday) could be quite strong and that could be negative for the market," said Sloan.
Economists estimate that industrial production jumped 0.6 percent in December after a 0.9 percent November gain.
December international trade numbers, which will figure into calculations of already strong fourth-quarter GDP (gross domestic product) forecasts, also come out on Friday.
"Medium term, there are still risks to the market," said Sloan. "Greenspan will be speaking next week and the week after, we get employment cost data and fourth-quarter GDP."

"I don't think the market has a huge amount of upside," said Sloan. "It will be difficult to move above 111-18 on the March T-bond contract. That was support before the strong December payrolls number. We could maybe get as high as 112-04 if we got supportive numbers."
At those levels, selling could emerge as participants square positions before Friday's data and next week's two- and five-year auctions, traders said.
The 30-year Treasury bond, which was up 9/32 to 96-17/32, yielding 6.77 percent in early trade.
Two-year notes were unchanged at 99-20/32, yielding 5.95 percent.
Three-month bill rates were down one basis point to five percent. Six-month bill rates were unchanged at 5.06 percent. Year bill rates were down one basis point to 5.26 percent.
-- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1679
